topic.rationale: Select the distant-earthquake/Devils Hole story for its immediate place-and-distance surprise and a payoff explaining what traveled, what moved locally, and why even small waves matter. Apollo 12 offers greater acute human stakes; the person-switch story offers direct self-relevance and a memory twist; RNA editing offers molecular wonder. At equal access and cost, the cave story most clearly converts one vivid observation into physical and ecological understanding. This is editorial judgment, not predicted retention, a water/physics preference or renderer convenience.

narration.text: An earthquake nearly four thousand miles away made waves in this Nevada desert pool. On July twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-five, a magnitude eight point eight quake struck off Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. Twenty-one minutes later, water in Devils Hole began sloshing. But seawater hadn’t crossed the ocean into Nevada. Seismic waves traveled through the ground. As the ground moved, water already inside the cave rocked back and forth—like water in a shaken bathtub. That oscillation is called a seismic seiche, different from an ocean tsunami. The waves here were about ten inches. Small, but enough to disturb a shallow shelf where the endangered Devils Hole pupfish feed and spawn. This event removed some material from the shelf. The park described it as a minor disturbance. An isolated-looking pool can reveal just how connected the ground beneath us really is.
